analysis.one_liner: Charges fossil fuel companies a rising carbon fee and rebates most of the money to lower- and middle-income households.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a single cosponsor, and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would put a fee on oil, natural gas, and coal starting at $25 per metric ton of carbon dioxide in 2023, rising $10 every year and faster if the country misses its emission targets. Most of the money collected would go back to adults as quarterly rebate checks, phasing out for households above $75,000 ($150,000 for couples). The rest would capitalize a new government financing agency for clean energy projects, pay farmers to adopt low-carbon practices, and fund job transition and cleanup grants for communities that depend on coal, oil, and gas work.
analysis.who_benefits: Lower- and middle-income households, who would receive quarterly rebate payments that generally exceed what a carbon fee adds to their energy bills, plus workers and towns in coal, oil, and gas regions who would get job training, early-retirement subsidies, and cleanup grants, farmers who would be paid for low-carbon practices, and communities facing pollution or climate damage, which would get priority for at least 40 percent of the new financing agency's grant money.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Lower- and middle-income households and energy-region workers

how_it_helps.text: Starting in 2023, companies that produce, refine, or import oil, gas, and coal would pay a carbon fee of $25 per metric ton of carbon dioxide, rising $10 each year and adjusted for inflation; if the country misses its emission targets, the annual increase would jump to $15, then $20, then $25.

Every adult would get quarterly 'carbon fee rebate' checks, phased out for individuals earning above $75,000 or couples above $150,000, with 75 percent of fund money going to these rebates in the first ten years.

A new Climate Change Finance Corporation would get $7.5 billion in each of fiscal 2022 and 2023 to fund clean energy, transit, and resiliency projects, with loan guarantees of 75 percent of loan balances, prevailing-wage rules, and Buy America requirements; at least 40 percent of grant funds must benefit low-income, pollution-burdened, and minority communities.

Communities and workers hurt by changes in carbon-intensive industries would get $5 billion in each of fiscal 2022 and 2023 for job training, apprenticeships, early-retirement subsidies, flood protection, and cleanup of coal ash, abandoned mines, and orphaned oil and gas wells.

Farmers, ranchers, and foresters would receive payments for practices that reduce emissions, with priority considerations for historically underserved producers, funded by 7 percent of fund money for the first ten years.

Imported fuels and carbon-intensive goods like steel, cement, and aluminum would face an equivalent fee, and exported goods would get refunds, so U.S. producers are not undercut by countries without carbon pricing.

analysis.who_pays: Oil, gas, and coal producers, refiners, and importers would pay the fee on every ton their fuels emit, heavy industries like steel and cement would pay fees on their process emissions starting in 2025, and these costs would be partly passed through to consumers in fuel and electricity prices before the rebate checks arrive; the Treasury would also appropriate roughly $85 billion up front to capitalize the fund and agency in fiscal 2022 and 2023.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and heavy industry

drawbacks.text: A carbon fee raises the price of gasoline, heating fuel, and electricity immediately, while rebate checks arrive on a different schedule, so households that drive long distances or lack bank or tax-filing access to receive payments could be squeezed in the interim.

The bill creates a new independent federal agency with a seven-member presidentially appointed board and wide discretion over tens of billions in loans, grants, and loan guarantees each year, a large and long-lived expansion of federal spending and bureaucratic power.

Energy-intensive manufacturing in steel, cement, chemicals, and glass would face new fees on process emissions from 2025, and although border adjustments would shield them from import competition, exporters in those sectors would still bear compliance costs.
No other senator of either party signed on, so the bill never demonstrated even the coalition a carbon tax would need to survive a Senate where such proposals have historically failed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design follows the classic 'fee and dividend' structure: because 75 percent of the money goes out as flat per-person rebates phased out only at middle incomes, most households below the phaseout threshold would come out ahead, since lower-income families use less fuel on average than the per-person rebate they would receive. The main honest costs are the transitional squeeze on energy prices before rebates flow, real compliance costs for fossil fuel and heavy industry, and the scale of a new $7.5 billion-a-year financing agency whose project choices would rest with a politically appointed board. It is a coherent progressive design, but it was introduced without any cosponsors and had no realistic path to passage.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in March 2021, never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the bill on March 10, 2021, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor at any point during the two-year Congress.
The Finance Committee took no further action on the bill, and no vote was ever held in either chamber before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers, refiners, and importers, along with heavy industry, are better off because they never faced the $25-per-ton-and-rising carbon fee, and oil, gas, and coal-dependent regions never faced the transition the bill would have funded. Everyone else simply kept the status quo, without either the fee or the rebate checks.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers and major emitters

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and got it referred to the Finance Committee; it was the only bill he put his name on here and he attracted no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance (Chair Ron Wyden)
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill for the remainder of the Congress — no hearing, no markup, no vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: Only one senator — a Democrat — ever supported the bill on the record; no Republican or other Democrat cosponsored it, and no votes were ever taken, so no partisan breakdown exists.

industries.industry: Oil, gas, and coal producers, refiners, and importers
industries.note: The bill directly taxes every metric ton of carbon dioxide their fuels would emit, starting at $25 and rising indefinitely; their only relief is a refund for carbon they actually capture and store. Their interest in stopping the fee runs against the public interest in cutting emissions, since the fee's revenue funds consumer rebates.

industries.industry: Heavy industry (steel, cement, aluminum, chemicals, glass, pulp and paper)
industries.note: These industries would pay fees on process emissions from 2025, but the bill refunds fees on exports and charges equivalent fees on imports, protecting them from cheaper high-carbon foreign competition — a structure that raises their costs while shielding their market position.

industries.industry: Clean energy developers and green banks
industries.note: A new federal financing corporation with $7.5 billion a year of startup capital would direct grants, 75 percent loan guarantees, and credit enhancements into solar, wind, geothermal, batteries, EV infrastructure, and grid modernization, creating customers and deal flow for the clean energy sector on terms the public would share in through emissions cuts and jobs.

industries.industry: Banks, credit unions, and community lenders
industries.note: The new agency would guarantee 75 percent of eligible loans made by federal and state-chartered banks, credit unions, community development financial institutions, and minority depository institutions, shifting clean-energy lending risk onto the federal government while lenders keep servicing roles and fees.

Farmers, ranchers, and foresters would be paid for verifiable practices like cover crops, conservation tillage, and manure management to ease their transition toward carbon markets, with extra consideration for historically underserved producers.
